225.title: Keep one line of Marcus
225.hook: twelve books to himself: death, duty, kindness, the whole
225.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius copy out a single line from the Meditations and keep it on a card, a wall or a lock screen, rereading it each morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the book's last section: the actor dismissed after three acts. Your line was three acts is a play. Did you let the acts you've had count? Day two hundred twenty-five.

When you finish a long book, what do you actually keep? Usually not the plot. Usually one sentence. One line that stuck to you, that shows up years later when you're stuck in traffic or can't sleep. We've now walked through all twelve books of Marcus Aurelius's notebook, written in Greek and addressed, again and again, to himself. Death, duty, kindness, the whole. Before we leave him, one job. Today, keep one line of Marcus.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU KEEP FROM A BOOK?` → `ONE LINE THAT STICKS.` → `TWELVE BOOKS, ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Let's walk back through the notebook, quickly, like flipping pages. Book one: his debts. From my grandfather, from my mother, from whom I learned. Then time. You've been putting it off, and there is a limit. Do each thing as if it were the last. Live three thousand years or three, and you only lose this moment. Then beauty in the wrong places: the cracked loaf, the split fig. Stand upright, not propped up. The inner retreat, open at any hour. Nature loves change. Like the vine, do good and move on. The mind is dyed by the thoughts you keep. The obstacle becomes the way. A purple robe is sheep's wool dyed in shellfish blood. Don't be turned into a Caesar. What isn't good for the hive isn't good for the bee. You'll meet the future with the same reason you have now. Then a plain one. In George Long's 1862 translation: "Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig." Then: it's not the thing, it's my view of it. A bitter cucumber? Put it down. Of course there are rude people. Stop arguing about what a good person is; be one. Like leaves. Graft back. Kindness is invincible. And three acts can be the play. Notice the four threads that keep returning. Death, used to wake up the present. Duty, the work in front of you. Kindness, even to difficult people. And the whole, the sense of being one small part of something vast. You don't need all of them. You need one.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose your line, and then copy it out. Settle and breathe. Let the lines drift past again. The cracked loaf. Dig within. Kindness is invincible. The obstacle becomes the way. Wait for the one that tugs. Don't pick the wisest. Pick the one you need. Repeat it slowly inside, three or four times, until it feels like yours. After the bell, write it down by hand. The bell holds the time.
Keep one line of Marcus. Twelve books to himself, about death, duty, kindness and the whole; one line is enough to carry. Today's word.
screen: `KEEP ONE LINE OF MARCUS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: keep one line. Today, write your Marcus line by hand, and put it where you'll see it tomorrow morning: a mirror, a wallet, a phone case. Day two hundred twenty-five.

226.title: Keep one story of Rumi
226.hook: longing, the beloved, the Prophet, the Quran, being cooked
226.howItsDone: In Persian-speaking and Turkish Sufi circles, the Masnavi is read aloud and explained story by story, often in weekly gatherings, and its tales are retold in homes and sermons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, twelve books of Marcus, flipped like pages. Your line was keep one line. Which one did you write down, and where did you put it? Day two hundred twenty-six, the end of the week.

Yesterday it was one line of the emperor. Rumi's Masnavi hands over something else to keep: not a sentence, a picture. A reed crying. A parrot playing dead. A lion leaping at his own face in a well. That's how Rumi taught: a story, then another story tucked inside it, then a turn toward God, then back to the story. The stories are how his teaching travels from one person to the next. So today's job is not to choose a quotation. Today, keep one story of Rumi.
screen: `NOT A SENTENCE: A PICTURE.` → `STORIES INSIDE STORIES.` → `KEEP ONE STORY.`

segments.voice: Let's walk back through the stories. The reed flute, cut from the reedbed, crying to go home: longing as a direction. The king and the handmaid, and the physician who found the real cause of her sickness when her pulse leapt at the name Samarkand. The grocer's parrot, who decided every bald man must have spilled oil too. The lion and the hare, where the animals say trust God and the lion says effort is God's way too, echoing the saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, about trusting God and still tying your camel. The merchant's parrot, who played dead and flew free. The old harper, playing for God alone in a graveyard, found and seen by the caliph Umar. Moses and the shepherd, and the voice that told Moses he was sent to join people to God, not to part them. The elephant in the dark, each hand touching only part. The chickpea in the boiling pot, told the heat is making it good. The Chinese and Greek painters, and the wall polished into a mirror. The lover at the door who learned to say it is you. The guest house. Ayaz and his old shoes. Now notice the threads. Longing: we're all parted from our source. The beloved: God, and the friend through whom God showed up. The Prophet and the Quran: story after story leans on a verse or a saying, and tradition says the poet Jami called the Masnavi the Quran in the Persian tongue. And being cooked: a saying often attributed to Rumi sums up his life as raw, then cooked, then burned. Every story is heat doing its work.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: retell your favorite story, to yourself first. Settle and breathe. Let the stories drift past: the reed, the parrot, the lion in the well, the chickpea. Wait for the one that won't leave. Then tell it inside, in your own words, beginning, middle and turn, as if to a child at bedtime. Not perfectly. Just alive. The bell holds the time.
Keep one story of Rumi. A reed, a parrot, a chickpea: his teaching travels as stories of longing, the beloved, the Quran and being cooked. Today's word.
screen: `KEEP ONE STORY OF RUMI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: keep one story. Today, tell your Rumi story out loud to one person, over dinner, on a call, in the car. A story only lives if it's told. Day two hundred twenty-six.

227.title: Beware the fake Rumi
227.hook: many viral "Rumi quotes" aren't his, so always check a translation
227.howItsDone: Readers who care about Rumi's words look for a line's place in the Masnavi or the Divan-e Shams and compare translations by people who read Persian, such as Nicholson or Arberry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the reed, the parrot, the chickpea. Your line was keep one story. Who heard your Rumi story? Day two hundred twenty-seven, and the last week of camp four.

You've seen them. A sunset photo, a curly font, and underneath: Rumi. Wedding toasts, yoga studios, a friend's bio, a tattoo on someone's forearm. Rumi is often called one of the best-selling poets in America, which is remarkable for a thirteenth-century Muslim scholar who wrote in Persian. But here's the awkward part. A good share of the lines passed around under his name aren't his at all, and many others have drifted a long way from what he wrote. Today, beware the fake Rumi.
screen: `A SUNSET, A CURLY FONT: RUMI.` → `A BEST-SELLER IN AMERICA.` → `BUT IS IT HIS?`

segments.voice: How does a fake Rumi happen? Three ways, mostly. First, the loose version. In the late twentieth century, some English poets who didn't read Persian made free versions of Rumi by reworking older scholars' translations. Some are beautiful poems in their own right. But they're often closer to the new poet than to Rumi, and they tend to leave out God, the Prophet and the Quran, the very things Rumi's lines were built on. Remember our rule from the start of this camp: keep him whole. Second, the drift. A loose version gets shortened, then paraphrased, then misremembered, until a sentence with no source at all is floating around with his name on it. Third, the pure invention: an inspiring line, usually in modern self-help language, that someone simply attached to a famous name because famous names get shared. How can you tell? Here's the honest method. Ask where it's from. A real Rumi line lives somewhere: a book and line of the Masnavi, or a numbered poem in the Divan-e Shams. Then find it in a translation made by someone who read Persian. Reynold Nicholson's translations, from 1898 on, and E. H. Whinfield's 1898 abridged Masnavi are old and careful. If you can't find the line anywhere but on posters, be suspicious. And notice the tone. If a supposed Rumi line sounds like it was written for a mug, with no God in it and no longing, that's a clue, not proof. Checking isn't being fussy. It's respect: for a real man, a real faith and the real words.
screen: `THE LOOSE VERSION.` · `THE DRIFT.` · `THE PURE INVENTION.` · `WHERE IS IT FROM? WHO TRANSLATED?` · then, large: `CHECK THE SOURCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one quote you love, starting now. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind a line you love, from Rumi or anyone. Say it inside. Then ask it three quiet questions. Where exactly is this from? Who translated it? Does it sound like the writer, or like the poster? You don't need the answers yet. Just notice how much you know, and how much you've trusted. The bell holds the time.
Beware the fake Rumi. Many viral lines are loose versions, drifts or inventions; a real one has a place in the Masnavi or the Divan. Today's word.
Your line: check the source. Today, take one quote you've shared or saved and look up where it really comes from. If it's not who you thought, that's worth knowing. Day two hundred twenty-seven.

228.title: Two men, two worlds
228.hook: a Muslim mystic in love and a Roman emperor on duty: different aims, different gods, kept apart
228.howItsDone: Careful readers of old texts keep each author in his own setting, reading Marcus as a Roman Stoic and Rumi as a Muslim Sufi, rather than blending them into one teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fake Rumi: loose versions, drift and invention. Your line was check the source. Did one of your favorite quotes turn out to be someone else's? Day two hundred twenty-eight.

It's tempting, after seventy-odd days, to blend them. The emperor and the poet. Both wise, both old, both on the inspiration shelf. You could make a nice poster: Marcus says this, Rumi says that, same idea really. But put them in a room together and they'd barely understand each other. They didn't share a language, a century, a god or a goal. We've read them side by side on purpose, and we've kept them apart on purpose. Today, before the camp closes, let's say why. Two men, two worlds.
screen: `THE TEMPTATION TO BLEND.` → `SAME IDEA, REALLY?` → `TWO MEN, TWO WORLDS.`

segments.voice: Start with the facts. Marcus Aurelius was a Roman emperor of the second century who wrote his notebook in Greek. Rumi was a Muslim scholar and mystic of the thirteenth century who wrote in Persian. More than a thousand years stand between them. There's even a small irony in the name. Rumi means of Rum, the name Muslims gave to Anatolia, because it had once been Roman land. That's the closest the two men come to touching. Now the worlds. Marcus's world is Stoic. The universe is ordered by reason, which he calls nature, or the gods, or Zeus. The good life is living in line with that reason: doing your duty, being just and kind, accepting what comes. He's honestly unsure what happens after death. Rumi's world is Islamic and Sufi. There is one God, Allah, known through the Quran and the Prophet. The good life is love: the reed longing for the reedbed, the lover burning to meet the beloved. His whole poetry leans toward union with God. So one man steadies himself; the other longs to be undone. One reaches for duty; the other for love. When they seem to say the same thing, like accepting what comes, they mean it for different reasons and aim it at different ends. Blending them would quietly erase both, the way many popular versions have stripped out Rumi's Islam. Keeping them apart lets each be himself. You can learn from both without making them agree. That's the line.
screen: `AN EMPEROR, A MYSTIC, A THOUSAND YEARS.` · `RUMI: FROM RUM, ONCE ROMAN LAND.` · `REASON AND DUTY; GOD AND LOVE.` · `LEARN FROM BOTH, BLEND NEITHER.` · then, large: `THEY DON'T MERGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one line from each, side by side. Settle and breathe. Bring back your Marcus line from three days ago. Let it stand on your left, in its tent by the Danube. Then bring back your Rumi story. Let it stand on your right, in Konya, with the reed flute. Don't make them talk to each other. Just let both be there, each whole. After the bell, write one line from each. The bell holds the time.
Two men. A Roman emperor on duty and a Muslim mystic in love, a thousand years apart, read side by side and never merged. Today's word.
Your line: they don't merge. Today, when you hear two wise people quoted as saying the same thing, ask what each one actually meant. Day two hundred twenty-eight.

229.title: How to keep reading
229.hook: a few lines a day, one line carried: the way to read any old book
229.howItsDone: Some readers of old texts read a few lines a day and carry one phrase, as Seneca describes in his second letter; Christians who keep lectio divina read scripture in the same slow way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the emperor and the mystic, a thousand years apart. Your line was they don't merge. Did you catch two voices being blended? Day two hundred twenty-nine.

There's a kind of book that ends up on a nightstand. A big old one, bought in a burst of good intention, read for three nights, then used as a coaster. Maybe the problem isn't the book, or the reader. Maybe it's the method. Old books get read the way the news gets read: fast, for information, all at once. They were never written for that. For seventy-odd days this camp has read two old books a few lines at a time. Today, how to keep reading.
screen: `THE BOOK ON THE NIGHTSTAND.` → `READ LIKE THE NEWS.` → `HOW TO KEEP READING.`

segments.voice: The Roman writer Seneca, a Stoic who wrote long before Marcus, gives this advice in his second letter to his friend Lucilius. Don't wander through piles of authors, he says. Stay with a few great ones and digest them. Food that comes straight back up doesn't nourish anyone. In Richard Gummere's 1917 translation, he puts it in three words: "Everywhere means nowhere." Then Seneca describes his own habit. Each day, out of everything he reads, he picks one thought to chew on for the rest of the day. And in that very letter he does it, picking a line from another philosopher, Epicurus, about poverty that's content being an honorable thing. One thought, carried. Christian monks worked out something similar. A medieval Carthusian monk named Guigo described a ladder of four steps for reading scripture slowly: reading, then turning the words over, then prayer, then resting in silence. It's called lectio divina, holy reading, and it is still practiced today. Different aims, different sources, the same rhythm: slow, little, and kept. So here's the method for any old book, sacred or not. Three lines a day. Read them slowly, twice. Pick one phrase. Carry it until evening. That's all. Three lines a day is more than a thousand lines a year. The Meditations, the Masnavi, the Psalms, the Gita, the Dhammapada: none of them has to be finished on a weekend.
screen: `EVERYWHERE MEANS NOWHERE.` · `ONE THOUGHT, CHEWED ALL DAY.` · `LECTIO DIVINA: FOUR SLOW STEPS.` · `READ SLOWLY, PICK ONE, CARRY IT.` · then, large: `THREE LINES A DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read three lines slowly. If there's a book nearby, open it anywhere and take three lines. If not, use three lines you know by heart. Settle and breathe. Read or say the first line, word by word, as if each word cost money. Then the second. Then the third. Now go back, and let one phrase rise. Hold just that phrase for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
How to keep reading. A few lines a day, read slowly, one phrase carried: Seneca's habit, and the monks' holy reading. Today's word.
Your line: three lines a day. Today, choose the old book you'll keep reading after this camp, and put it where your phone usually sits at night. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

230.title: Hundreds more
230.hook: the Masnavi has hundreds of stories, and we read about twenty
230.tomorrow: camp 4 close: the reed and the emperor
230.howItsDone: Readers who love Rumi keep going through the Masnavi one story at a time, in Persian or in translation, often with a teacher or a reading circle, for years.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Seneca's one thought a day and the monks' slow reading. Your line was three lines a day. Which old book did you set by the bed? Day two hundred thirty.

A visitor finishes one shelf of a huge old library, heads for the exit, and the librarian at the door says: that was the lobby. That's where we are with Rumi. Across this camp we've read about twenty of his stories: the reed, the parrots, the lion, the harper, the shepherd, the chickpea, the painters. But the Masnavi runs to six books of verse, and it holds hundreds of stories, many nested inside each other. We've barely opened the door. Today, hundreds more.
screen: `ONE SHELF, AND IT WAS THE LOBBY.` → `ABOUT TWENTY STORIES.` → `HUNDREDS MORE.`

segments.voice: Here's a taste of what's waiting, all from book one alone. A proud grammarian gets into a boat and asks the boatman, have you ever studied grammar? No, says the boatman. Then half your life is wasted, says the grammarian. The boatman goes quiet. Then a storm rises, and the boatman asks: have you ever learned to swim? No, says the grammarian. Then all your life is wasted, because the boat is sinking. Rumi's point, drawn out over many lines: in the deep water, cleverness about words won't hold you up. What saves you is emptying yourself, becoming like the dead, who float. There's a man from the city of Qazvin who goes to a tattoo artist and asks for a fierce lion on his shoulder. At the first prick of the needle he cries out: which part are you doing? The tail, says the artist. Leave off the tail, says the man. Then the ear. Leave off the ear. Then the belly. Until the artist throws down his needle and says: who ever saw a lion with no tail, no head and no belly? Rumi's point: you want to be a lion, but you won't bear the needle. And there's a deaf man who goes to visit a sick neighbor, rehearsing polite answers in advance, and gets every one hilariously, painfully wrong. That's three stories. There are hundreds more. Rumi himself breaks off some stories mid-way, doubles back, picks them up again later. It's a book to live in, not to finish. E. H. Whinfield's abridged English Masnavi from 1898 is old enough to be free to read, and Reynold Nicholson's full translation followed in the twentieth century.

Hold it. Ask what it might say about you this week. Don't solve it. The bell holds the time.

231.title: Camp 4 close: the reed and the emperor
231.hook: seventy-five days with two books; next, the depths
231.howItsDone: Readers who have finished a long reading of Rumi and Marcus often keep both books near: Rumi for longing and devotion, Marcus for daily duty, read a few lines at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the grammarian in the storm and the lion with no tail. Your line was hundreds more. Did you find a story we didn't read? Day two hundred thirty-one, the last day of camp four.

Seventy-five days ago, you picked up two books at once. One by a poet in Konya who wrote in Persian and, tradition says, dictated his book to a student. One by a Roman emperor, written to himself in Greek, some of it, the book's own headings say, in army camps on the northern frontier. Two men who never met, a thousand years apart, who would have found each other strange. We've carried both, and kept them apart. Today we close the camp and name what we found. Camp four close: the reed and the emperor.
screen: `TWO BOOKS, SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS.` → `KONYA, AND A CAMP ON THE FRONTIER.` → `THE REED AND THE EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: Here are the camp's words, in the order we met them. Masnavi, Rumi's long poem of stories, in six books. Sufi, the Islamic mystical path he walked, and our promise to keep him whole, Quran, Prophet and all. Ney, the reed flute crying for the reedbed. Tawakkul, trust in God, with the camel still tied. Daimon, Marcus's divine spark within, to be honored and kept upright. Ghazal, the love poem signed with Shams' name. Sema, the turning, listening with the whole body. And Şeb-i Arus, the wedding night, a death kept as a meeting. Around those words, the two men gave us two great moods. From Rumi, longing. The reed sings that whoever is parted from their source longs to go back, and that ache isn't a malfunction; it's a direction. From Marcus, duty. Do the next thing in front of you, justly and kindly, without hurry, as if it were the last. Longing pulls you toward what you love. Duty keeps your feet on the ground where you are. They don't merge, and we won't pretend they're one teaching. But a person can carry both, the way you can carry a compass and a lantern. And now, the depths. Camp five is the last camp of this year.
